utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Good morning, everybody. Madam Registrar, could you kindly call the case, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. This is the case number IT-05-88-T, The Prosecutor versus Vujadin Popovic et al.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. Thank you, ma'am. All the accused are here. From the Defence teams, I only notice the absence of Mr. Bourgon. The Prosecution, Mr. McCloskey and Mr. Thayer. Are there any preliminaries? Yes, Mr. Ostojic.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. President, Your Honours. There is one preliminary.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Good morning to you.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. President and Your Honours, we have what we believe is a serious concern. I know from time to time, we've raised issues with the Court. We just yesterday, at about 10.00, received the Prosecutor's motion in connection with Witness PW-108. Without naming him, obviously, and discussing it, it seems to us that the Court has been advised of this witness for some time since, I believe, August and February, when you initially made your ruling. Our concern is that Zvornik witnesses, specifically like this gentleman, Mr. Jovicic, has come here and we will not have an opportunity, because at least the accused Beara, we did not have any information in connection with this witness and the witness with whom he had this hearsay conversation who is now deceased in order to question this witness. We've not been able to investigate any of the allegations made by this witness or by the witness who he spoke with, and other witnesses perhaps. So --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: You're still referring to 108?

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: 108 and the declarant who apparently passed away, whose name I don't know if I can reveal or not, so I'm not --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: No, no, I would prefer you didn't for the time being, just to be on the safe side.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: I just wanted to direct the Court to it. And we believe that it's obviously shifting the burden on to the Defence to bring witnesses here -- the burden of proof, to bring witnesses here and not to allow us to have an opportunity to cross him on what seems to be critical evidence, I think it causes prejudice, and it's quite candidly, without overstating it, and I think I'm understating it, it's trial by ambush. If they had this evidence as early as August of 2006, there should have been at least a conference with the Court by way of a pre-trial conference or at least a conference with counsel to advise us of the evidence. If the Court will note, when they made their application initially, they identified PW-108 very nondescriptly and very benignly, similar to how some of the witnesses have identified certain accused in this case. We were not put on notice, and yet before the trial started there was clear evidence in the possession of the Prosecutor which goes to acts, purportedly, and conduct against our client. Secondly, it doesn't seem that the Prosecution, with all due respect to them, has abided by the Rules of Procedure and Evidence in this trial. If they had evidence of not just this declarant, PW-108, but of the deceased individual, which seems to exist, meaning his prior statements, which are more than one from what I can gleaned from reviewing this briefly yesterday and this morning, as well as possible other testimonies that this deceased person gave in this Tribunal, it should have been offered to the Court, at the very least --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Please slow down.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: I apologise, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: No, no, I could follow you, but obviously you're going too fast for the interpreters, so if you could kindly slow down a little bit, I think it will help.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: I know we've raised this issue with other witnesses, but I think to give the Court one statement without giving the Court the benefit of these other statements, and the fact that PW-108 may have testified in another proceeding which I just learned about this morning - I haven't checked the accuracy of that - in another Chamber. I think the Court needs to have the benefit of the complete picture, and I think the Defence, by not getting any information in connection with that, has been prejudiced from cross-examining other Zvornik Brigade members, witnesses, who have testified. By way of example, with this witness, Your Honour, I think it would have been appropriate if we were given this information in a timely manner to consult with our client, to find out whether there is any truth to these allegations which are clearly prejudicial, and clearly can impact not only the Court's view here as well as what witnesses may say. We don't have identification of these individuals. We would ask that a photo chart or photo identification board be presented so I can ask this individual, for example, Mr. Jovicic, if he ever saw these people coming at any time in July of 1995, among some of the questions that we would ask. Failure to be given this information, this witness will be gone forever and will not be able to be recalled to ask those questions. This witness, again by only one example, was present in the Zvornik Brigade on a regular and continuous basis, at least according to his testimony. He would have and should have, in our view, at least noted that there was some people from the outside, as the Prosecution purports, who have come into the Zvornik Brigade to investigate or to try to have meetings or consultations with various members of either Zvornik or other corps or commands. When I use the word "ambush," Your Honour, I know we've used it before, it truly is a trial by ambush, and what it does is ultimately result in our, the Defence attorneys, in our case, at least, to be giving ineffective assistance of counsel to our client. We cannot, if the Court is seized with information this critical, be able to have our case presented when the Court has information that we, as Defence counsel, don't even know about, that our client has no information about, because from at least my review of this person's statement, there was never any contact specifically with Mr. Beara. It's trial by ambush because it prejudices our rights to be able to come to the Court with any - thank you - with any sense of credibility to tell you what we think the facts are and how we think the inferences should be applied. This evidence, we suggest, should have been given to us very early in the case, before even August of 2006, which is before the trial proceedings. I know this witness gave a statement in August of 2006, but we should have had the deceased declarant's statements, plural, as well as his purported testimony - if it's accurate that he gave that testimony - well before the trial started so we can consult and properly advise and inform our client of his rights. So I'm suggesting today that we suspend the proceedings with respect to this witness and any other Zvornik Brigade witnesses until we've had ample time to obtain from the Prosecutor all the documents in connection with PW-108 and this deceased individual, as well as the documents, the physical documents that this deceased person apparently gave to his brother that's mentioned in the statement, whose name I can give the Court in private session if the Court desires. We're only given one statement with various conclusions. Even if we were to apply Rule 92 quater, it doesn't in my view, respectfully -- it's not applicable because 92 quater clearly says that if it goes to the acts and conduct of the accused, the Court may look at that as a reason not to admit certain evidence of a declarant. We don't believe it's applicable in this case. We urge this Court, and I know we've asked you for many things and have been rejected on some and we've been granted some motions that we filed, it's an important issue because we have not had an opportunity to consult with our client, with our co-counsel in this case, and I believe that there is grave prejudice that's being committed in this Chamber with respect to this trial by giving this Trial Chamber specifically information and facts and not sharing it with the Defence or the Defence attorneys. So that's my request, Your Honour, this morning. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you. Who is going to respond to that? To be precise, you -- just in case anyone has any doubts in their mind, we're talking of the motion which was filed yesterday evening, or yesterday, anyway, and that's a confidential ex parte motion on the part of the Prosecution on 14/5, and then the annex, which is the annex part of the document referring to who would be Witness PW-108, and that would be Witness number 166. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: That's correct, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: And when is he scheduled or she scheduled not just to give any information, when is the witness scheduled to testify?

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: I advised my learned colleague, Mr. President, that we will be issuing our schedule today. I believe he is scheduled to testify 18 and 19 of June.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Eighteen or 19 of June. All right, so we have another month from -- another month from now. I noticed Ms. Nikolic on her feet. Yes, go ahead, Ms. Nikolic. And I will give you an opportunity to respond as soon as I hear also what Ms. Nikolic has to say. I presume on the same subject, isn't it? Yes, go ahead, Ms. Nikolic.

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Your Honours, and thank you. Before I respond to the Prosecution, maybe it would be a good idea for this Defence team to complete its presentation regarding the latest situation. I fully join in everything that Mr. Ostojic said on behalf of his client, and I subscribe to it in full, especially with regard to the witness Mr. Jovicic who is to be cross-examined today. The Defence teams have prepared for cross-examination limited only to the evidence we have so far. However, in the present situation, the minimum that I would request would be to delay cross-examination for 24 hours in order to enable us to consult with clients, to present them with the statement of Witness PW-108, and in view of that, to prepare for further cross-examination. In addition to that, in this trial at least three or four witnesses have been heard from the staff of the Zvornik Brigade who were present in the building of the staff in Karakaj during the critical events, and if we had known about all these circumstances we would have questioned them about certain personalities such as Witness 108 and 102. Therefore, I fully support Mr. Ostojic in what he said, and I believe that this way of disclosure is prejudicial to the Defence and could affect the fair and equitable trial of our clients.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Thayer. Do you wish to respond?

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. Good morning to you and Your Honours. Good morning, everyone. Just initially, with every best wish to the current witness, I hope nobody is gone for good once they leave the Trial Chamber. The fact is that any of these witnesses can be recalled at a later date, and what is important, I think, to note, and as we've discussed already, the 30-day notice in this case is specifically designed to delay the disclosure about which my friends are complaining, but the Prosecution believes it has ample good-faith basis for seeking that delayed disclosure, and that is why it has come at this time. If I may move into closed session, Your Honour, or private session just for a moment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, by all means. Let's go into private session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: We are in open session.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And I'll just repeat a little bit of what I said in closed session. The circumstances surrounding the application for delayed disclosure with respect to this witness, PW-108, are precisely those anticipated by the delayed disclosure rule. With respect to my learned friends' concern about ability to cross-examine adequately the current witness, again, this witness can be recalled at a later date on that very limited issue. We have currently scheduled this witness to appear 19 June. The exhibit list in connection with PW-108 will be part of this afternoon's filing. That will come, clearly, too late, I think, to cross-examine this witness with anything that's on there that's not contained in the statement that's already been disclosed to Defence counsel, unless we keep this witness here for however long my learned friends believe they need to prepare. This is not trial by ambush. This has never been trial by ambush, Your Honours. This is the Prosecution reacting to the assassination of a witness and taking every full measure it can to make sure that that does not happen to any of its other witnesses. There was simply, given the court schedule or given the trial schedule, the way the witnesses have developed, and this is when this witness fell into the witness order. We have complied with the rule. If my learned friends feel that there is any witness that has been called that they need to question about the identity of this witness, then we will make every effort to bring those witnesses back. I think that is about as much as I can say on this issue at this time, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Ostojic.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, we've raised our voices and we've been very emotional at times, and quite candidly I think it's not fair, and it's not fair and what Mr. Thayer has now said is just -- as we have from time to time have said, is just not accurate. The information, just from gleaning on PW-108's statement is clear, that the witness that they claim was assassinated, for whatever the reason is, whether it was an involvement, they're trying to make a connection with his testimony here. I don't know anything about the assassination. It's the first time I'm hearing about it now. However, looking at PW-108's statement, it's clear that the statement itself that this deceased individual gave had the name of a pseudonym on the statement. It removed any identity of who this individual is. They could have, if they wanted to, without prejudicing our rights and without violating the right of equality of arms in this trial, without committing a trial by ambush, they could have given us those documents of the deceased individual with as many or as few redactions as they previously have done with other instances. It's just not accurate to represent to this Court at any time that they are trying to protect a witness because a witness came to this Tribunal in order to get -- and was assassinated as a result of that. I don't have that information, but it's inaccurate to say that, "Our hands were tied and couldn't produce that to the Defence counsel." They had other means, both by rules and as innovative as they are with how they present evidence to this Trial Chamber, I must say I feel that the Trial Chamber has been prejudiced by reviewing this and allowing us, as Defence counsel, ineffectively to assist the accused and our clients in this case, by taking one route, while the entire time they are filing ex parte and confidential annexes with the Trial Chamber, with very vague statements as to who these individuals are and not even telling us who the conduct of the statements that they are presenting of witnesses may or may not relate to. I do not find that Mr. Thayer's comments, quite fairly and respectfully to him personally, are accurate and fair. The witnesses' statements that they had of the deceased individual did not reveal his name. That's what I can glean from PW-108's interview. They could have provided it to us. They could have provided us a summary as they have in their 65 ter list. They failed to follow any rule of procedure in this Court. If we had known this information, we would have perhaps taken a different route on the defence. To suggest that there is a remedy that we can call witnesses back is simply an attempt to try to shift the burden of proof to the defendants, and I can try to explain as to how. We're not having this trial in a piecemeal fashion where we can bring a witness in and say, "Yes, Judge, I forgot to ask a question. Can we bring him back in?" All the witnesses, quite candidly, if you look at it, should be brought back for further examination. That would be, quite candidly, a miscarriage of justice if we did that. It's not a remedy to bring a witness back. We shouldn't even discuss a remedy. They should have given us the statements in a redacted version or in the version that they currently have, with the pseudonym of this individual, so the Defence in August prior to -- or I should say in July of '06, prior to the commencement of this trial, had all the evidence as it is prescribed by the Rules of Procedure and Evidence in this case. It's patently not fair; the Prosecution knows it's a trial by ambush. That's why they sit here and they give the Court annexes which are ex parte. We objected to the filing in August when they made the application only because we sensed that there was just something unfair. I invite the Court to look at the filing and what they say about PW-108. They describe it in a very benign manner. They do not tell us, the Defence counsel, who this witness may or may not be against. They could have done that without prejudicing or waiving any rights that they have. Counsel, I respectfully say, does not have the right to say that we have an ability to cross-examine the witness unless he's put in that place. I invite the Court, if you're going to do anything, to suspend the proceedings and order that the OTP produce all documents, not just the witness statements that we have now, but the prior witness statements, the testimony of this witness that is deceased, as well as the records that this witness has -- that had in connection with what purports to be his investigation. I urge this Trial Chamber to do it so that we could try to proceed, and I don't know -- and I truly believe but I think it might be too late, but try to proceed and have a fair trial in this case. But I think that it may be too late and that the Prosecutor has prejudiced the rights of all the accused here. Thank you, Mr. President and Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Ostojic. Do you wish to comment any further? And there is one or two questions I would like to ask you. Obviously, I think I'm speaking for myself, but this motion has basically appeared before us this morning and I notice now that it has got, amongst it, annexes, statement interview -- OTP interview statement which goes back to 2006. Again, I may be asking a question based on my lack of full information, but is there a reason why you annexed that statement to the motion?

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: I think I can answer, Your Honour, and I can be honest with the Court, why they gave it to you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, but I'm asking Mr. Thayer for the time being, not you, Mr. Ostojic. If you don't agree with his answer, then -- please sit down.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Your Honour, I wasn't part of the filing of the motion, but the best answer I can give Your Honour is I think that's consistent with our prior practice with respect to these sensitive witnesses. We've only filed, I think, one or two other such motions for delayed disclosure. When we've done that, we've attached these documents to give the Court a full understanding of the context as to the importance and sensitive nature of the Prosecution's application. We offer that so that the Court can make its decision based on appropriate and full -- as full information as we can provide in the filing.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: What I mean -- I think my question has been misunderstood or I didn't put it clear enough. The question of delayed disclosure is a matter that we decided earlier on already. On that occasion, again, I can't even rely on my memory now because I definitely don't have a recollection of it. We might have had, as an annex, the statement. But now we have come to a stage where the identity of this witness is being disclosed in accordance with our decision, that is, 30 days prior to his expected testimony, and that's why I asked you, because basically you gave an indication of the week of 11 June, but not a specific indication that I wanted to know, so why give us again the statement?

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Your Honour, the honest answer is, beyond what I said, I'm not sure. We may have provided it just to give the Court -- remind the Court what the context was. It may have -- if I may consult with Ms. Stewart for one second. I just need to find out whether it was --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. And the other question is: Would the existing statements of the deceased person, the one you qualified as assassinated, have they been disclosed to the Defence or not?

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Those have not been disclosed, Your Honour. To the extent that PW-108 would be referring to them, I believe that those may be part of the exhibits that will be listed today on the Prosecution's June filing.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right, thank you. Yes, Mr. Ostojic.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, I just don't understand what they're trying to do. PW-108 was asked questions, and all they did was read from the deceased person's statements. It's clear, I'm ashamed to tell the Court that if you had this statement, I feel the Court truly should have taken a different route. I don't know if the Court had it. I know you had a confidential annex. I hear from the Court, on page 15, that -- and I'm not sure if I heard you correctly, Your Honour. I hope you didn't have this statement all the way before in August, because I -- oh, thank you. I see some nodding and I wasn't sure of that. We don't know what the annex is. For Mr. Thayer to suggest to this Court that, "We didn't give the statements because this witness is going to testify on his own," let anyone look through PW-108's statement. They clearly only read -- they read from the deceased individual's thing to confirm whether or not he saw something. I not only want the statements, I respectfully request that we get the testimony, and I would like on the record to know which case it is and if he testified live or if he testified under a pseudonym, which pseudonym number it is in the other case. We can go into private session for that. And I want to know the documents that this deceased individual and his brother apparently continue to have in their possession in his home -- the brother, I should say, has in his home. It's clearly -- the answer to your question is: Prejudiced. This Trial Chamber needs to be prejudiced. That's what Mr. Thayer should have said. That's why they attached the annex --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Slow down, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Slow down.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: That's why they attached the annex to the motion. There is no reasonable avenue or option or reason logically that they would have attached this statement other than to poison the well, quite candidly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. I think we've heard enough. We need to suspend the sitting for a short while.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Mr. President --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So one -- perhaps you can first give us an answer why this statement --

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Yes, and I --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: -- was appended now when, to our knowledge, at least, it was never appended before, so --

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: I asked leave to consult with Ms. Stewart because I wanted to find out --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Fortunately, we have not read it. I mean, I speak for --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Didn't have time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Didn't have time, but yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: It seems the Court reads many statements before we do, so that's why we assumed the Court did, with all due respect.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: We only saw the motion -- actually, it was on our desk this morning when we came in, and we simply never had the time to even -- in fact, I brought it here with me, seeing that it is a motion requesting protective measures more than anything else, to find out when this witness is coming to give evidence and to see whether there would be the usual no-opposition response from the parties; and that gives you an indication of how much we have read from the motion. So, yes, Mr. Thayer.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And to that extent, Your Honour, I'm in somewhat the same boat. Having just looked at the motion, the best answer I can give the Court is: As it is a motion for protective measures, attaching the statement seems to be a logical way of providing the Court with the factual grounds in seeking actual protective measures for this witness once he's here, understanding that the Court has already granted the delayed disclosure and there's been a certain amount of analysis that's gone, we can't just rest on that in seeking actual protective measures for the motion. I imagine that's the reason why the statement was filed. If I can add just one other piece of information. From quickly looking at the prior filing, it appears the statement was not appended to our prior application, just I think a 65 ter summary and that was it, so I just wanted to clarify that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I think that's clear for the record, because the practice varies from Chamber to Chamber here, and there are some Chambers who insist in having these and other similar documents beforehand. We have chosen the other way, and we have chosen the other way not to show any criticism to the practice as adopted in other Chambers, but because we believe that is the practice that we should adopt for this Chamber, and I would leave it at that. But that's across the board. I mean, if you had filed it in the first place when you had the first motion for delayed disclosure, we would have reacted more or less the same, the same way. I mean, it's -- we're not talking of mortal sins here. It's a question of a choice that we have made not to be -- not to have at our disposal, before a witness starts, his previous statements, unless we're talking, of course, of a 92 ter or a 92 bis witness. And the last thing, Mr. Thayer, the last point: These statements of the deceased person, if he was intended as a witness, as it seems to be, was he, according to you, assassinated when he was about to travel to give evidence in this case or in another case?

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Your Honour, my understanding is he was killed prior to --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. I think we can leave it. Go ahead, we can stay in open session, yes. And the reason why I want to really know is if he was a witness intended to testify at this trial, how come his previous statements have not been disclosed to the Defence, if I have understood you correctly, because I am beginning to wonder if I'm understanding the whole picture?

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: I think we're all on the same page with respect to this point, Your Honour, and that is my understanding is that the witness who was killed was killed prior to the filing of the Prosecution's 65 ter witness list. That is my understanding. If we may move into private session just for a brief moment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay, then let's go into private session, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: My understanding is --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: One moment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, go ahead. You can start again, Mr. Bourgon, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. The idea we will not mention either the name of the deceased person, but what I will say is that on numerous occasions the Prosecution has used the death of this witness as a reason to obtain protective measures for witnesses in this case. The Defence has opposed the information which was provided by the Prosecution, which was pure speculation. On the other hand, we have provided the Trial Chamber with newspaper clips that would clearly establish that this witness had been killed in the context of being a witness (redacted), nothing to do with this Tribunal. Of course, the Prosecution opposed that and they say that's not true. And what my colleague just said, that he was on his way to be a witness here or to be interviewed here, I don't have the exact wording. To my recollection, what the Prosecution mentioned in its filing is that the witness was due to be interviewed, but in any respect, whatever the Prosecution said, it is in writing in the filings that they presented before this Chamber. Now, what I wanted to say at this point in time, Mr. President, is that the issue - and I join with what Mr. Ostojic just said - the issue is we do not know what information was in the possession of the Trial Chamber, because there was some information in this annex that was appended to the motion. And we opposed strongly the fact that we were not told not only the identity, not only the statement, not even the topic of the statement, and against which of the accused in this courtroom this person was due to testify. We were completely in the dark. Our motions were denied. So be it. The Trial Chamber can rule on it. At a later point, and I can't recall now if this was before the ruling of the Chamber or immediately after, I stood up again before you, asking to know -- I said, "Mr. President, we are going -- we are taking the wrong route, whereas there's a witness out there, we don't know who he is, we don't know what he will say, we don't know against whom he will testify, and we need to be told at least some information." Now, at this point in time we -- it is too early for us to tell how serious this violation is, but for sure we are of the view that there is a severe violation of the rights of the accused. And at this point in time, while it's too early to take any measures or for any filings or for any requests, our only request at this time, at least we can consult with our clients, at least share the information which must have been said before I arrived, is only in English and not in the language of the accused, so that the accused has to read that information, that we can sit down with them, take instructions, and at the same time do a proper analysis of the motions that were filed previously, what the decision of the Chamber was, and then we can tell you tomorrow morning what is the course of action. But my colleague has already expressed what our request is in terms of Zvornik Brigade witnesses as well as in respect of this witness that is in the box today, and as a minimum, Mr. President, we respectfully request an adjournment until tomorrow morning, where we can address you and tell you exactly what our position is after we've had time to properly take instructions from our client. Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated] As I see it, because I think certain arguments are going beyond what would appear to be strictly relevant. The statement you now have, and it has been disclosed in accordance or pursuant to our previous decision of the late disclosure, so you have it. What you don't have is any possible previous statements of the deceased persons, and that is, I think, what is at the crux of the matter. Madame Fauveau, and I will give you the floor, and you, Mr. Ostojic, and then we conclude, please. Yes, Madame Fauveau.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I just wanted to say a few words about a restricted subject. I support completely Mr. Bourgon, and I want to add, concerning the death of this witness, when this person was killed last year, the Prosecution himself admitted that he had no evidence that this person was killed in connection with this Tribunal or his evidence before this Tribunal. I find it extremely offensive to us, the Defence, that every time the Prosecution needs it, he raises this issue, because by raising this issue, the killing of this witness, allegedly linked with the Defence, the Prosecution implies in a certain way that the Defence could be implicated, while having absolutely no evidence of that. I hope that the Prosecution will stop referring to this killing without presenting any evidence that this killing is in any way related to this Tribunal or the testimony of this witness before the Tribunal. I believe that every future reference to this murder, implying that it is somehow connected to this trial, should be seen as pressure on the Defence, because we are already under other pressures, and I believe that the inference that this Defence is somehow implicated or involved or related to this is insulting.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I had seen you standing, Mr. Ostojic. Do you wish to add anything or --

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Without repeating, Your Honour, I just want to pointer out --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I hope so --

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: I won't, Your Honour, but I just wanted to point out to the Court, the Court asked the pointed and specific question to the Prosecutor, "Why did you attach the interview," and he seemed to indicate that it was some custom and practice. And I wanted to raise with the Court -- and the Court was correct in saying he could have simply done it in a paragraph to share what fears this witness may have, he could have talked to the Defence counsel who have been, I think, quite candidly, more than reasonable in not objecting to requests for pseudonyms or voice or face distortion. We've not been unreasonable in any of their requests, and I strongly believe, not only in my heart but in my gut, but I strongly believe that there's only one reason why this annex was attached. And I would ask this Court to return that motion and to return that annex, so the Defence can have an ample opportunity to decide what exactly our next step or tactic might be. One final point that I think I failed to mention with respect to my client Mr. Beara, I have not consulted with him on this. We came in this morning. We got it last night. We were yesterday in the UNDU until 8.00 meeting with him on other matters. This motion was given to us late. I think he has an opportunity, although Mr. Thayer talks about prejudice and he talks about protecting other witnesses, and bringing other witnesses -- this trial and the proceedings and the rule is to protect the accused's rights, and those are, first and foremost, the rights that we should be looking to protect. The Office of the Prosecutor never raises those issues because we think and we believe that we know what their opinion is in this regard, and now their actions I think have spoken louder than words by producing and giving to this Trial Chamber such a statement without even consulting with us or even discussing it with the Trial Chamber, and giving it to us in piecemeal form. Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you. Any further last comments, Mr. Thayer?

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Your Honour, just three brief items I need to raise. The first one is I need to ask for a redaction at page 20, lines 20 to 24.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: One moment. Let me follow you. Page --

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Page 20 of our LiveNote, lines 20 to 24. There is a reference to another specific case or trial, and I --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Why should it be redacted?

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: If I may go into private session just briefly, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. Let's go into private session.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Mr. Bourgon --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: One moment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Let's go back to open session -- to private session, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: My second point, Your Honour, is I wanted to respond to the query from Your Honour and the issue raised by my friend concerning the statements and other exhibits in connection with the deceased witness. We will make all of those materials available. As I said, I believe those materials will be part of the exhibit or statements package, related materials, with respect to PW-108, so that material we will get to the Defence. They will have that. The only issue is will they have it in time, for example, for the current witness on the stand to be able to process and prepare for cross-examination. Finally, Your Honour, with respect to the Court's discomfort with the annexation of the statement, if the Court wishes to completely disregard the statement in the context of its decision, we understand that. We can make whatever submissions are necessary without referring to the specific statement. We understand that. We -- and we will be guided by the Court's preference and practice in that regard.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. Please, let's conclude this so that -- before you speak, let's take a decision on the redaction and then continue and finish the debate.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So let's go to private session for a very short while, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Bourgon.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Very shortly, Mr. President, to try to close the debate, my colleague has just mentioned, and I quote his words, "We will make all those materials available," and a couple of lines down, I'm quoting from page 29 now, lines 8 to 10: "The only issue is will they have it in time, for example, the current witness on the stand to be able to process and prepare for cross-examination." Mr. President, what the issue is before you this morning and what the Prosecution fails to grasp is that the new information we have been served with yesterday has a bearing and an impact on a number of witnesses that have appeared thus far before the Trial Chamber, and this is what we need to assess, this is what we need to discuss with our clients, and this is what we need to argue before a Trial Chamber at a later time to see what is the proper remedy for this new information that comes more than halfway through this trial. And this, we believe, was done voluntarily not for protective measures, this was done voluntarily as trial tactics on behalf of the Prosecution. This is our opinion, this is what we believe in, and this is what we will argue as part of our arguments tomorrow. Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay, thank you. I think we can suspend now the sitting for some time, until we discuss and deliberate. Okay. We'll let you know exactly when we will reconvene, because obviously I haven't got a clue as to how much time we require to discuss, but I anticipate a minimum of about 20 minutes, at least, something like that. --- Break taken at 10.06 a.m.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So we are reconvened. I notice the absence of Mr. Meek. I don't need to put on record -- they are coming; okay. Then I don't need to put on the record that Mr. Bourgon showed up during the previous session because his interventions speak for themselves and for his presence. All right. We'll try and address the various issues that have been raised and decide them. First, we deal with the question or the request that has been made for the postponing of the testimony of the present witness, the one who was testifying yesterday and with whose cross-examination we should have continued, as well as the request that has been forecast as to the possible recalling of the need to recall and further cross-examine previous witnesses. Our position and our decision is as follows: With this current witness, Vojicic -- What is his name?

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Jovicic, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Jovicic, and, for that matter, any other witness that the Defence may wish to cross-examine further in the light of the statement to the OTP of would-be Witness PW-108, and the statements of the deceased witness whose name I am not going to mention but who is mentioned in the Prosecution's confidential motion of yesterday, the Trial Chamber will make a provision for such further recalling and cross-examination once an ad hoc request is made by any of the Defence teams and accepted by the Trial Chamber. In the meantime, however, we will proceed with the cross-examination of the mentioned -- the above-mentioned witness, Jovicic. We come next to the would-be Witness PW-108, 108's statement to the OTP, the 2006 statement attached to the Prosecution confidential motion already mentioned, that is, the one which was filed yesterday, and with which we became familiar this morning. Given the preference that the Judges composing this Trial Chamber have indicated at the start of trial, the Trial Chamber does not require the said statement and decides to expunge it from the records. We also enjoin or invite the Office of the Prosecutor not to file such material with this Chamber in future unless such material is specifically asked for by the Trial Chamber, although we do appreciate that it is an accepted practice with other Chambers to have such statements attached to motions. The reason -- we also wish to make clear that the reason for our choice is our preference, individually, and I say "individually" because in the beginning I made it clear that everyone -- every Judge in this Trial Chamber was free to adopt a different system if she or he wished to do so, but the four of us agreed to adopt a uniform system. The reason for our choice is our preference for direct and oral testimony and not because of any concern that we would be biased if we had such material available beforehand and if we read it beforehand. I wish to make this clear. The Trial Chamber wishes to add that none of its members have read the statement attached to the Prosecution's confidential motion filed yesterday, and that the same statement did not form part of the 2006 Prosecution motion for delayed disclosure. You will recall that we had decided that motion on the 9th of February of this year, and any future reference to that decision is specifically to the 9th February decision. The Trial Chamber, however, wishes to disassociate itself from any suggestion that the filing of such material such as previous statements of witnesses is improper or that adherent in such filing is the intention to unduly influence the Judges. In other words, we are disassociating ourselves completely from deducting from the fact of such filing the intention to unduly influence the Judges. With reference to the statements of the deceased person, again I won't mention his name, we require the Prosecution to disclose to the Defence that material without further delay. Finally, we come to the criticism that some Defence teams have levelled at the Trial Chamber's previous decision on the late disclosure. It is now the decision of the 9th February 2006. Such decisions are never the preference of the Defence, but they are sometimes necessary and are provided for by our Rules. The Trial Chamber has already taken its decision, striking a proper balance between -- a proper balance in accordance with the Statute, Rules and jurisprudence of this Tribunal, and we have nothing else to add to this. So that disposes of the various matters that have been raised, and we are now ready to continue. Mr. Bourgon.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. Mr. President, we take good note of the Trial Chamber's decision. However, I would like to maybe seek clarification with respect to Annex A which was joined to the motion -- the annexes which were joined to the Prosecution motion requesting this additional witness. This material is necessary for us in order to assess the situation, and we believe, Mr. President, that the situation is more serious than what is being considered presently, and this material is required for us to assess.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I think, Mr. Bourgon, I mean, we can say very little on this. It has been filed as an ex parte, and once it is filed an ex parte, I mean, we can't change the nature of that filing. It's up to the Prosecution to decide whether they want to give it to you or not, and perhaps you may have consultations with the Prosecution on that. But once it has been filed ex parte, we cannot change it into confidential or to a public filing.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Mr. President, I think I need to address the Trial Chamber. I don't know if the witness has to stay here or to remove his earphones, but --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I don't think it is appropriate for the witness to be present for this discussion that has got nothing to do with him, also to put his mind at rest that we are not discussing him and we haven't been discussing him, basically. We've had some procedural problems to address this morning which were not anticipated. I had no idea yesterday that we would have these problems today, and that is why you have been kept waiting outside in that room. So please, Mr. Jovicic, please accept my apologies for that, but I need you to understand that we need to conclude our discussion on these issues before we can continue with your testimony. This has got nothing to do with you, basically. I mean, we're talking of other issues. So I would suggest -- do you understand English? All right. So I suggest that he leaves the courtroom again, and we'll be calling you back in about five to ten --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: One moment, one moment. Judge Prost has come up with a better suggestion, namely, to go ahead and finish the cross-examination of this witness and then we address the matter that you raised, Mr. Bourgon, immediately after.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: I take it, Mr. President, that then there will be a possibility for us to recall this witness, because --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I think I have already stated, in the beginning of our decision, that both as regards this witness and others that you may wish to recall for further cross-examination, we'll decide those matters once we are seized with an ad hoc request, and of course it is at least, on the face of it, a justified one. So let's continue. We've decided to continue our discussion after we finish with your testimony first.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yesterday we had come to the Beara Defence team which had asked for a postponement, so Mr. Meek, I suppose, if you are ready, we can proceed with your cross-examination, and then the Nikolic and finally the Pandurevic Defence teams.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Good morning, Witness.

utterances.speaker: MILANKO JOVICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: How are you today?

utterances.speaker: MILANKO JOVICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Very well, thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Sir, you were telling us yesterday that one of the functions of an operations duty officer would be to make a written account in the logbook, such as the logbook that you have in front of you now, that you had sent out a request or an order, for example, to a battalion; is that correct, sir?

utterances.speaker: MILANKO JOVICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't send a request to the battalion, but I am obliged to record everything that comes in through the duty telephone, as the operations duty officer. I only had a request for the R Battalion. I don't recall the order, but I did read it because the duty operations officer can receive an order that he would need to read to all of the battalions or to the individual battalions.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Sir, would it be fair that as an operations duty officer, you might receive a call, for example, asking you to contact a person in a battalion and request -- or give them information, for example, or check on a situation? Would that be a fair statement?

utterances.speaker: MILANKO JOVICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can receive a request or a call as operations duty officer to call somebody who's supposed to call back or to convey the request to him, but then I would need to note down what I received and what I conveyed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Sir, thank you. I think that's how I understood your testimony. So in the normal course of your job description you gave yesterday, as an operations duty log officer, you're expected to respond or acknowledge the request which has been made or passed through you, whether it's been completed if you hear back; is that true too?

utterances.speaker: MILANKO JOVICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is correct. I was obliged to convey it, that is all. I don't know about whether it was completed or not. The person who was supposed to do it would need to report back once it was completed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: And, sir, wouldn't that happen on a lot of occasions or most occasions?

utterances.speaker: MILANKO JOVICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know. I wasn't the operations duty officer frequently, so I cannot really say if this would happen a lot or not.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Now, if it did happen, though, and it came through you, you would -- as you testified yesterday, it would be one of your obligations to write that down, what you were told?

utterances.speaker: MILANKO JOVICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Now, I noticed that in the book that you have in front of you, which is P0070 --

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: -- 377, it's important, is it not, that you, as a duty operations officer, would make your notations with an ink pen? Is that correct, sir?

utterances.speaker: MILANKO JOVICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is how I did it. I used an ink pen.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: And I noticed in -- I notice, sir, in your statement that you gave to the Office of the Prosecutor, that they showed you this logbook from the Zvornik Brigade and you looked through it, and you observed some of your handwriting; is that correct, sir?

utterances.speaker: MILANKO JOVICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: And we've looked at that yesterday. The reason -- let me ask you, the reason you would use ink is so that the messages you receive or that flow through you and come back to you, perhaps, cannot be erased, changed, modified or falsified? Would you agree with that, sir?

utterances.speaker: MILANKO JOVICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is quite logical.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: And if you could, sir, would you just briefly look through the exhibit in front of you, the actual Exhibit P00377, and flip through there and tell me, sir, isn't it true that the notations in that book, starting from the first page on, are in ink?

utterances.speaker: MILANKO JOVICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, so that you don't have to wait any more, 90 per cent or almost 95 per cent of what I looked at is written in ink. Perhaps if an ink pen ran out or something, there would be some pencil, but then as soon as they got a fresh pen, they would continue in ink. I think there's only one paragraph that is just written in pencil.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Thank you, sir. Now, as I understand your testimony yesterday, you had a practice that when a shift was finished, that -- meaning your shift, from perhaps 6.00 to 6.30 in the morning, the duty officer would come back on duty and they would write the date and then start making their own entries; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MILANKO JOVICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: [No interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: And, sir, what is the importance of writing the dates?

utterances.speaker: MILANKO JOVICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The date is written so that you could see who was on duty when. Every day, you would write in the date of the duty shift.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: And it would be normal, would it not, that you would write the date in one time for each day as they began at 6.30 or so in the morning when the duty officer came back on duty; is that correct, sir?

utterances.speaker: MILANKO JOVICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Before you continue, Mr. Meek, if you look at the transcript, page 39, the previous page, line 20, we do not have on the record the witness's answer to your question, and I think we need it. You need it, we need it.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: I heard it, Judge, but I'll ask it again.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So did I, I heard it, too, but my attention has been drawn that it is missing from the transcript.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: I appreciate that, Judge, because I didn't see it.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Sir, I asked you that the practice that you had was that when a shift was finished, that meaning your shift, perhaps 6.00 or 6.30 in the morning, and then the duty officer came on that morning, the duty officer would write the date and then start making their own entries after that, and I asked you, "Is that correct," do you remember that question?

utterances.speaker: MILANKO JOVICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, you did ask me, and that was the practice. The assistant operations duty officer would be on duty until the operations duty would come back, and then when he came back, he would write down what he needed to write down.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: And isn't it also true that another reason that it's very important to write that date down is to memorialise what occurred during that 24-hour period, roughly; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MILANKO JOVICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Now, I think in your testimony or your statement, you indicated that you had looked through the logbook that you have in front of you, P00377, and you didn't notice any irregularities; is that a fair statement or not?

utterances.speaker: MILANKO JOVICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Now, could I just briefly have you look at the 14th of July in the book you have in front of you, sir. And for e-court purposes, B/C/S version would be with the ERN number ending with 5744 [Realtime transcript read in error "5754"], and the English version would be ending 9339. Could those be placed on e-court side by side?

utterances.speaker: MILANKO JOVICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: What page is that on?

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Okay. It would be on the top, sir, you see some stamped numbers on the top of each page?

utterances.speaker: MILANKO JOVICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I see it, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: 5744 [Realtime transcript read in error "5754"]. Okay? Do you have that in front of you, sir? We don't have it on e-court yet.

utterances.speaker: MILANKO JOVICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I see it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay, all right. I think it's --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Page 7 in English?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Can you help us with that, Mr. Meek, or Mr. Thayer?

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: The ERN number for English is 03089339 in the English translation. What page it's one, I'm not sure.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: That's page 7 of the English translation, I believe, and page 126 of the document on e-court, if you can locate that page.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay, thank you. Thank you both.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Can we have them side by side? Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PROST
utterances.text: Mr. Meek, before you go on, I think this could confuse us in future. The transcript in two places is talking about ERN ending 5754, but I believe what you said is 5744. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PROST
utterances.text: Just so we have it clear when we go back to these pages.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: I'm sorry. I apologise. That's correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you. It's probably not your fault. Thank you, Judge Prost.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: If you take a look at the date on that page, it's down towards the lower right-hand corner, I believe. You can scroll down -- there you go. What does that say, sir?

utterances.speaker: MILANKO JOVICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: "The 14th of July, Jokic."

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: And for the Trial Chamber's information, is that "14 July, Jokic," is that written in pen or in a pencil?

utterances.speaker: MILANKO JOVICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Pencil, normal pencil.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Okay. Now, what time was that jotted down?

utterances.speaker: MILANKO JOVICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Let us just clarify something. I was looking at my texts in this book, and you asked me if that was correct. I am not qualified to assess whether the whole logbook is correct. I'm not qualified to assess if somebody put something incorrectly. I have said I'm not a professional soldier. I have a civilian education. I'm a civilian. I really apologise to the Court, but ...

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: No, I understand that, sir. I'm just asking you because you've done this work, and you've already testified yesterday about how important it is to put times the calls came in and the date, so all I'm asking you is just to look and tell me if you can tell me what time that call came in, from your knowledge and experience. That's all.

utterances.speaker: MILANKO JOVICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I cannot tell you because I was not on duty at the time. I can tell you that when I was on duty, each call was recorded.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Okay. But this -- would you agree with me there is no time on this notation?

utterances.speaker: MILANKO JOVICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is evident. You can see from the book that it's not there.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Now, if we could just turn to the very next page on both B/C/S and English, which would be, in the B/C/S version, 5745, and English, 9340. Okay, thank you very much. Sir, you notice that the very next page, at the top left corner, it has again another date, 14 July; correct?

utterances.speaker: MILANKO JOVICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Is that also --

utterances.speaker: MILANKO JOVICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Normal pencil.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Now, and I want you to help me here, sir, if you can. If we go to the very next page in B/C/S and in English, the B/C/S would be 5746, English 9341, thank you, it appears to me -- two questions. One, there was a message taken at 1024 hours, "Asmaci [phoen] informed Lieutenant Davicic [phoen], about the movement of Muslims." Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: MILANKO JOVICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: And apparently there's approximately seven hours till it goes to the next entry at 1500 or 3.00 p.m., and there's a notation that says: "Colonel Beara is coming"; correct?

utterances.speaker: MILANKO JOVICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Maybe you can help me here, but in those times and especially in the period that we're talking about from the 12th through the 19th of July, 1995, isn't it odd, sir, that there would be seven hours with no radio traffic or no entries in the two logbooks?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: One moment, one moment.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, then, you should ask the operations duty officer who was on duty at that time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: One moment. Yes, Mr. Thayer.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Just a slight clarification for the record. If 1500 represents the time, it's five hours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: This is what I was going to ask, why seven hours. I mean, it's --

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Well, I'm not a mathematician, Judge. It's my fault. I apologise. Five hours' difference is what I meant, if you know.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Mr. Ostojic already admitted to not being one himself, so that you are in good company.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You would need to ask the operations duty officer who was on duty at the time, why he didn't write down anything. I'm not qualified to assess or evaluate why he didn't write anything down.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Thank you, and I appreciate that. Do you have any idea, if you can help me, who would that duty officer have been that day, so I could ask him?

utterances.speaker: MILANKO JOVICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not a handwriting expert, and I cannot recognise or recollect handwriting.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Okay, thank you very much. We're going to go to the very next page, which would be the 5747 in B/C/S and 9342 in English. Thank you. Witness, since you have the original notebook in front of you, can you confirm we're still on the same day, the 14th of July? I need you to scroll down on the B/C/S, please.

utterances.speaker: MILANKO JOVICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There is no new date put anywhere, so if we're looking at the handwriting, it should be the same. But to tell you the truth, I'm really not a handwriting specialist, and there is no date written anywhere.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: We can conclude, though, can't we, sir, that there will not be another date until the next shift comes on in 24 hours? That's what you've testified to, I believe.

utterances.speaker: MILANKO JOVICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There is no date here. I don't know where the next date is. We would then need to look to see when the next shift started. You have the book, so you can check that yourself.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: I'll just ask you, I'll ask you real quickly, just for your own purposes go to the page that's got the 5753 real quickly, about four pages over probably in that book. We don't need to put it on the ELMO right now or the e-court. It's on the left side, sir.

utterances.speaker: MILANKO JOVICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Which part did you say?

utterances.speaker: MILANKO JOVICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it's there.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: And what does that say, sir, "15 July 1993-- 95"?

utterances.speaker: MILANKO JOVICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Is that in pen or is that in pencil, sir?

utterances.speaker: MILANKO JOVICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Normal pencil.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: So going back to the page we had before, which was 5747, and in English, I'm sorry, it would be page 10 of the English translation or 9342, and if you scroll down a little bit on the English. That's fine, that's fine, okay. Now, there again on the 14th, at 1500, there is a call logged in, "Curkin should pass via Sekovici." Correct? 1500 hours, you see it? Again, sir --

utterances.speaker: MILANKO JOVICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes, I see it.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: The first question there: Is there any way you can explain how two calls came in at exactly 1500 hours, the one on the page before that said: "Colonel Beara is coming," with other information, and then: "Curkin should pass via Sekovici," at the same time?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Thayer.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: I think the witness has indicated he is limited in the ability for him to interpret other people's entries. At this point, I would object.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: No, just let him answer. If he's in a position to answer it, let him answer it. If he's not, he's intelligent enough to tell us.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It's not logical to have two entries that are the same at 1500 hours, but again I apologise to this Honourable Court. I'm not qualified to evaluate the work of others. I can only speak about my own work. I'm really sorry.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Thank you very much. And, sir, there's nothing to be sorry about at all. Now, just move on -- look on down that page, sir, after -- four or five lines after "730-312 Zlatar".

utterances.speaker: MILANKO JOVICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: That's an entry, is it not, that says: "At 1400 hours, connect relay Palma 2"; am I right about that?

utterances.speaker: MILANKO JOVICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It says here: "At 1400 hours," I don't know what this is, "Palma 2," and then I cannot really decipher what it says at the bottom, I can't tell if it says "Vukotic" or "Vukocic", I can't really tell --

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: That's fine. I'm more interested in the timeline --

utterances.speaker: MILANKO JOVICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Excuse me. "At 1400 hours, the situation regular, Palma 2, at 1400 hours, the situation regular, Palma 2." I can't tell what it says at the bottom, "Vukotic," "Vukocic," I can't really don't know what it says. Maybe somebody called in that the situation at Palma 2 was regular.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Thank you, sir. And real quickly, right above that line, you see the name Ljubo Bojanovic, do you not?

utterances.speaker: MILANKO JOVICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: And who is that person, if you know him?

utterances.speaker: MILANKO JOVICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Ljubo Bojanovic died. He was the duty operations officer. He was a major of the Army of Republika Srpska.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Thank you, sir. Now, if you could just go to the very next page in your book. I'm sorry to have you put your glasses on and off, like you are. 9343 -- I'm sorry, that would be English. 5748 in the B/C/S and 9343, page 11, English. That's fine. Do you see, sir, about six lines down, seven lines down or so, where it says again: "1500 hours"?

utterances.speaker: MILANKO JOVICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It could be "15.03" or it could be 1800 hours, you can't really tell, if you're looking at the second-last line, "Semso in preparation." I can't tell.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Witness, I want you to look on up that page, if you will --

utterances.speaker: MILANKO JOVICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It says: "1500 --"

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: That says "1500" there, does it not?

utterances.speaker: MILANKO JOVICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It says "15, 00". It can be something else. It doesn't say "hours." It could indicate something else.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: All right. Below you notice there is a "1503", did you not: "Semso is preparing" something?

utterances.speaker: MILANKO JOVICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I see it. It looks like a "5" and it doesn't look like a "5". Again, I say I am not a handwriting expert.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: And if you can tell me, again, we see: "13 July 1995" right about three lines above that, do we not?

utterances.speaker: MILANKO JOVICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Again, would you agree with me that it's illogical to have that three times now on three pages, the date?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Thayer.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Mr. President, I would just ask that the witness be permitted to read the entire entry that's related to that particular mentioning of the date.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Witness, take your time. If you need to read through what has been suggested, then please do so, by all means, and we'll wait for you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I've read it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay, thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This doesn't have to be the date of the duty shift. It can be that on the 13th of July, 1995, the UNHCR convoy for Srebrenica returned the same day and crossed into the FRY at 2305 hours, so it doesn't have to be the date. It just can mean that he received information that the vehicles of the UNHCR returned -- went and returned on that day.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you, sir. Now, if we move forward two pages -- three pages, excuse me, to the number 5751 in your book and page 14 in the English copy, ERN number 9346. First off, you'll agree with me we're still on the 14th of July? If you want to verify that, you can just flip a few pages in your own original book there and you'll see where the 15th of July starts, allegedly. The next page.

utterances.speaker: MILANKO JOVICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Okay. On the next page, it's the 15th, but it's written in pencil, which doesn't mean that it's precisely the 15th.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Well, that's a very good issue. Since it's written in pencil and everything else is in ink on that page, couldn't that -- doesn't that tell you there's something wrong with that, sir?

utterances.speaker: MILANKO JOVICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sir, let me tell you again. I'm not an expert in this, and I cannot competently discuss this. I'm really sorry, but that's the way it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Again, going back two pages to 5751, on the 14th of July still, we see another notation, correct, about halfway down the line, where it says -- first off, scroll back down, please. Keep going to the name "Jokic." Do you see the name "Jokic" there?

utterances.speaker: MILANKO JOVICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I see.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Could you read the entry for us, please?

utterances.speaker: MILANKO JOVICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It says: "Jokic, delegation from Pilica."

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Okay. Now, you'll agree with me that again there's is no time on that, is there? No one -- whoever wrote that down didn't put a time that came in?

utterances.speaker: MILANKO JOVICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: If you'll follow that page on down, you'll see the numbers "155". Do you see that, sir?

utterances.speaker: MILANKO JOVICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: And that says what, sir?

utterances.speaker: MILANKO JOVICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: "Beara should call."

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Okay. Call 155?

utterances.speaker: MILANKO JOVICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It says only, "At 155, Beara should call."

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: At 155. Thank you very much. As we go on down, if you'll go to the very next page, sir, with the numbers "9347", and that's page 15 in the -- I'm sorry, 5752 for you, sir, the next page, 9347 in the English translation, page 15. Scroll down a little bit. The B/C/S, scroll down again. I'm sorry. There. What time on the 14th does that notation say that Beara is coming?

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: If we go up above that, it says what before "Beara"?

utterances.speaker: MILANKO JOVICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: "Drago should call Mane - Djukici."

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, what I'm curious about, if you can tell me, is: Does this seem illogical to you, that on the 14th of July, at 1500 hours or 3.00 p.m., there's the same notation: "Colonel Beara is coming," and also at 9.00 a.m. on the same date?

utterances.speaker: MILANKO JOVICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sir, I told you, I'm not qualified to assess -- to evaluate the work of the duty operations officer.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Thank you, sir. And just on this, one more -- just flip one more page, sir, to 5753. I think we've already -- I'm going to ask one more time. I think it's been answered, Judge, and I apologise. The date, 15 July 1995, "15.07.95", that's in pencil, is it, sir?

utterances.speaker: MILANKO JOVICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, pencil.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: You may not be able to answer this, or maybe you can. Do you know who wrote this in pencil or why did they write it in pencil?

utterances.speaker: MILANKO JOVICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know. I don't know who entered this or why.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Given that the majority if not all of the dates are written in ink, doesn't it surprise you that these are written in pencil?

utterances.speaker: MILANKO JOVICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It does, but I can't explain it. I don't know why it was done that way.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Sir, do you know where the OTP received this notebook, how it came into their possession?

utterances.speaker: MILANKO JOVICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know how they got hold of it, but the logbooks or diaries were in the command of the Zvornik Brigade.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: At any time -- you're saying under oath that you have no knowledge, personal, direct or indirect, as to how the OTP came in possession of this notebook?

utterances.speaker: MILANKO JOVICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I testify under oath that I don't know how they got hold of this book. I was surprised to see it in their hands, and I don't know how they got hold of it.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: You testified yesterday that your direct superior was Dragan Obrenovic; do you remember that, sir?

utterances.speaker: MILANKO JOVICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: And did you ever have any discussions with Dragan Obrenovic at any time after these events and before he was arrested?

utterances.speaker: MILANKO JOVICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I had friendly conversations, and we sometimes had coffee together, but no more than that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Did he ever tell you that he kept that logbook in his own possession and then finally turned it over to the Office of the Prosecutor?

utterances.speaker: MILANKO JOVICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We never discussed that. It was never a topic between us.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Since he was your direct supervisor or superior, did you ever see any of his handwriting or writing enough to identify it, such as these dates in pencil, for example?

utterances.speaker: MILANKO JOVICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Twelve years is too long a time for me to recognise somebody's handwriting, plus I'm not good at remembering handwriting. I memorise telephone numbers because that's in my line of work, but far from that with handwriting.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Thank you. So I'm going to try to hurry up with this and ask you some "yes" or "no" questions so we can just finish.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Mr. Meek, just to enable you to regulate your cross-examination accordingly, since we had a long break that's almost one hour, but I understand that everyone else was in the courtroom before we arrived, I have consulted with the registrar what time we should have our next break, and she suggested, after consultation, 12.15. That's in five minutes' time. So I'm just giving you this information so that you know exactly how to go, how to proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: I appreciate that, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Mr. Jovicic, let's try to get through some things very quickly. You do not know where this logbook was or who had control of it from the time -- the last time you saw it until it was turned over to the Office of the Prosecutor; correct?

utterances.speaker: MILANKO JOVICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: When I left, in fact when I was demobbed from the Zvornik Brigade, I didn't know what happened with these diaries from that time on.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: We've talked about the 14th of July being written in twice. Can we look back to the 11th of July? And I understand, sir, that this is not your entry, and actually it's not even in an English translation, so, Witness, I would just ask you, and, Usher, if you could show 5728 in the B/C/S version, keep scrolling to the bottom -- there you go. Do you have it there in front of you, sir?

utterances.speaker: MILANKO JOVICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
